etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English brand, from Old English brand (“fire; flame; burning; torch; sword”), from Proto-West Germanic *brand, from Proto-Germanic *brandaz (“flame; flaming; fire-brand; torch; sword”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrenu- (“to bubble forth; brew; spew forth; burn”).

Cognate with Scots brand, West Frisian brân (“fire”), Dutch brand, German Brand, Swedish brand (“blaze, fire”), Icelandic brandur, French brand (< Germanic). More distantly cognate with Proto-Slavic *gorěti (“to burn”).

quote.citation: 1559, Jasper Heywood, transl., Troas:
quote.text: Goe to prepare the maryages what neede the torchis light? be holde the towres of troy do shyne with brandes that blase full bright.

quote.citation: 1559, Jasper Heywood, transl., Troas:
quote.text: Is yet againe thy brest enflamde, / with brande of venus might

definitions.definition: (archaic or poetic) A piece of burning wood or peat, or a glowing cinder.

quote.citation: 1513, Gavin Douglas, The Eneados:
quote.text: The fearful brands and bleezes of het fire.

quote.citation: 1859-1890, John Gorham Palfrey, History of New England to the Revolutionary War
quote.text: Snatching a live brand from a wigwam, Mason threw it on a matted roof.

quote.citation: 1835, [Washington Irving], chapter VI, in A Tour on the Prairies (The Crayon Miscellany; no. 1), Philadelphia, Pa.: [Henry Charles] Carey, [Isaac] Lea, & Blanchard, →OCLC, page 47:
quote.text: About three o'clock, we came to a recent camping place of the company of rangers: the brands of one of their fires were still smoking; so that, according to the opinion of Beatte, they could not have passed on above a day previously.

quote.citation: 1559, Jasper Heywood, transl., Troas:
quote.text: Or when amid the Grecians shippes, / he threw the brandes of fyre.

definitions.definition: (Scotland, Northern England) A torch used for signaling.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book X”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: Paradise, so late their happy seat, / Waved over by that flaming brand.

quote.citation: 1834 September (date written), Alfred Tennyson, “Sir Galahad”, in Poems. […], volume II, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, stanza I, page 174:
quote.text: The shattering trumpet shrilleth high, / The hard brands shiver on the steel, / The splintered spear-shafts crack and fly, / The horse and rider reel:  […]

definitions.definition: A mark or scar made by burning with a hot iron, especially to mark cattle or to classify the contents of a cask.

quote.citation: 1982 December 4, Mitzel, “A Sissy's Revenge”, in Gay Community News, volume 10, number 20, page 9:
quote.text: The indelible word "homosexual," like a brand that grew deeper and redder every day, became increasingly hard to conceal and to ignore.

definitions.definition: The symbolic identity, represented by a name and/or a logo, which indicates a certain product or service to the public.

quote.citation: 1999, Bernd Schmitt, Experiential marketing, page 39:
quote.text: The Amtrak brand revitalization approach represents one of the most ambitious, comprehensive, and systematic experiential marketing approaches I have ever seen.

quote.citation: 2000, Duane E. Knapp, The Brandmindset, page 67:
quote.text: In this way, every Citibanker becomes a brand manager and an ambassador of the Citibank brand. ... Indeed, the Citibank brand will "never sleep"

quote.citation: 2010, Gayle Soucek, Marshall Field's: The Store That Helped Build Chicago, page 136:
quote.text: Mr. Lundgren claimed that Federated had conducted a focus group and the analysis showed that most people were either indifferent to the name change or preferred the Macy's brand.

quote.citation: 2013 July 20, “The attack of the MOOCs”, in The Economist‎[1], volume 408, number 8845:
quote.text: Since the launch early last year of  […]  two Silicon Valley start-ups offering free education through MOOCs, massive open online courses, the ivory towers of academia have been shaken to their foundations. University brands built in some cases over centuries have been forced to contemplate the possibility that information technology will rapidly make their existing business model obsolete.

definitions.definition: A specific product, service, or provider so distinguished.
(by extension) Any specific type or variety of something; a distinct style or manner.

quote.citation: 2014 November 17, Roger Cohen, “The horror! The horror! The trauma of ISIS [print version: International New York Times, 18 November 2014, p. 9]”, in The New York Times‎[2]:
quote.text: [O]ne minute this "Jihadi John" was struggling to get by, and get accepted, in drizzly England, unemployed with a mortgage to pay and a chip on his shoulder, and the next he stands in brilliant Levantine sunlight, where everything is clear and etched, at the vanguard of some Sunni Risorgimento intent on subjecting the world to its murderous brand of Wahhabi Islam.

definitions.definition: The public image or reputation and recognized, typical style of an individual or group.

quote.citation: 2011, Tom Bevan, Carl M. Cannon, Election 2012: The Battle Begins, Crown, →ISBN:
quote.text: The Obama brand had taken a hit two months earlier, when he campaigned for Creigh Deeds in Virginia and Jon Corzine in New Jersey, only to see them both  lose.

quote.citation: 2012, Start Your Own Personal Concierge Service, Entrepreneur Press, →ISBN, page 104:
quote.text: Her brand is edgy, cosmopolitan, and out-of-the-box, so blogging is the perfect, ever-changing match for her.

quote.citation: 2019, Sally Thorne, 99 Percent Mine: A Novel, HarperCollins, →ISBN:
quote.text: He unplugged my umbilical cord to take a leisurely swig, smirking, watching me turn blue before giving it back. My cardiologist told me that was impossible, but I'm still convinced. That's very on-brand for [my twin] Jamie.

quote.citation: 2022 May 14, David Segal, quoting Simon Kuper, “An Outsider Takes an Inside Look at the Oxford ‘Chums’ Who Run the U.K.”, in The New York Times‎[3], →ISSN:
quote.text: “We made fun of [Jacob Rees-Mogg] in the paper” — that would be Cherwell, Oxford’s student-run weekly, where Kuper was a reporter — “all the while not realizing that we were helping to build his brand.”

definitions.definition: Any minute fungus producing a burnt appearance in plants.
(transitive) To burn the flesh with a hot iron, either as a marker (for criminals, slaves etc.) or to cauterise a wound.

quote.citation: 1880, Richard Francis Burton, Os Lusíadas, volume II, page 405:
quote.text: Man's flesh they eat: their own they paint and sear, / branding with burning iron, — usage fere!

definitions.definition: (transitive) To mark (especially cattle) with a brand as proof of ownership.
(transitive) To make an indelible impression on the memory or senses.

quote.citation: 1908, W[illiam] B[lair] M[orton] Ferguson, chapter II, in Zollenstein, New York, N.Y.: D. Appleton & Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: I had never defrauded a man of a farthing, nor called him knave behind his back. But now the last rag that covered my nakedness had been torn from me. I was branded a blackleg, card-sharper, and murderer.

quote.citation: 2011 October 23, Phil McNulty, “Man Utd 1-6 Man City”, in BBC Sport:
quote.text: As Ferguson strode briskly towards the Stretford End at the final whistle, he will have been reflecting on the extent of the challenge now facing him from the club he once branded "noisy neighbours".

definitions.definition: (transitive, marketing) To associate a product or service with a trademark or other name and related images.
(intransitive) To be very hot, to burn.

quote.citation: 1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, Canto II:
quote.text: O, not for thee the glow, the bloom,⁠Who changest not in any gale,⁠Nor branding summer suns availTo touch thy thousand years of gloom: […]
